clue.text: Obtained work on books that decay

parts.note: obtained means got, past tense of get
OP is short for opus, a musical or literary work
OT is the Old Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone acquired some writing about books that are rotting away.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the work stacks on top of the books.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to pot is an idiom for deteriorating or falling into ruin, which is what decaying things do.

clue.text: Queue at the hole in the wall? Hardly likely when you are on it!

definitions.text: Queue at the hole in the wall? Hardly likely when you are on it!

parts.words: Queue at the hole in the wall? Hardly likely when you are on it!
parts.note: bread is slang for money and a line is a queue, so a money queue at a cash machine (the hole in the wall); but anyone on this line is too poor to be withdrawing cash

explanation.surface: A wry remark that the poorest people rarely line up at a cash machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hole in the wall' is British slang for a cash machine. Being 'on the breadline' is an idiom for living in poverty, which is why a queue for cash is unlikely.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a subsistence level of income, historically the queue for free food handed to the destitute.

clue.text: Modern-day separation is out of control

parts.note: AD, Anno Domini, labels dates in the present era
a rift is a split or separation between people

explanation.surface: A remark that today's broken relationships are running wild.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat drifting without moorings or steering is uncontrolled, and the word extends to anything rudderless.

clue.text: Cabinet give award to directors

parts.note: a cup is a trophy awarded to a winner
a company's directors together form its board

explanation.surface: A government cabinet hands out a prize to company bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' suggests the government; here it is a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabinet is a piece of storage furniture with shelves and doors, the same thing as this kitchen item.

clue.text: Altering elements might bring it!

parts.note: the elements here are wind, rain and sun, so altering them is a shift in conditions; the surface hints at chemistry, swapping elements

explanation.surface: A chemist's boast that rearranging elements could bring about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The elements' is a common phrase for the weather, which kills the chemistry reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A shift in rain, sun or wind is exactly an alteration of the elements in the outdoor sense.

clue.text: Street where the prime minister receives everybody without exception

indicators.note: the prime minister receives a guest, taking the next word inside

parts.note: PM is the standard abbreviation for prime minister
everybody means all
without exception means all, every single one

explanation.surface: A London street where the head of government welcomes absolutely everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: PALL MALL is a famous street in London's West End, near the royal palaces and clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name of a particular London thoroughfare, so it is an example of a street.

clue.text: Monsters held up by some of the lesser gods

indicators.note: held up says the hidden letters are read backwards
some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Monsters are being detained by minor deities.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'held up' means read upwards, so the run SERGO from 'lesser gods' is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the giant man-eating brutes of fairy tales, a kind of monster.

clue.text: Speak disparagingly, if feeling tired and worn out

explanation.surface: Someone talks down to a person who is exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: To run something down is to belittle it, and a run-down person is exhausted and in poor health; a run-down building is shabby.

clue.text: Tied up soldiers in temper

indicators.note: in places the soldiers inside the word for temper

parts.note: a mood is a temper or state of mind
RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a corps of British army soldiers

explanation.surface: Troops in a foul temper have been bound and restrained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tied up' looks like a description of captive soldiers, but it is the definition of a boat secured at a quay.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat is said to be secured when its ropes fasten it to a buoy or quay, as a tied-up vessel is.

clue.text: Everybody you said to call is attractive

parts.note: everybody means all

indicators.note: said shows the next word is heard rather than read, giving its sound as a letter

parts.note: the word you is pronounced like the letter U
to ring someone is to telephone or call them

explanation.surface: A claim that anyone who phones you is charming.
explanation.definitionFit: Alluring means enticing or tempting, an equivalent of attractive.

clue.text: Contribution from party people

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party
a nation is a people sharing a country

explanation.surface: A political party's supporters provide a contribution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests politics; here it is a celebration, a do.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift of money or goods to a cause is a contribution, which is what a donation is.

clue.text: Pole accepting firm's lucky charm

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the pole takes the firm inside it

parts.note: a mast is a tall pole, as on a ship
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A Polish man takes a company's good-luck token.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' at the start of the clue looks like a person from Poland; it is a mast.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or object kept to bring good luck, like a charm.

clue.text: For a game one might go for a spin if allowed in the road

definitions.text: a game one might go for a spin

indicators.note: in puts the word for allowed inside the road

parts.note: a route is a road or way
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: A motorist's thought that a quick drive is fine if the road permits it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go for a spin' suggests a drive; in the casino game the wheel spins and players stake on where the ball lands.
explanation.definitionFit: This casino game is played on a spinning wheel, so a player effectively gambles on a spin.

clue.text: Happy to comply, though boiling over before midnight

indicators.note: before places the anagram ahead of the final letter
over suggests something knocked over, so the letters of boiling are rearranged

parts.note: the middle of the word night is the letter G

explanation.surface: Someone willing to help even though they are furious late at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' signals the anagram of 'boiling'; 'midnight' is the middle of 'night', and 'before' puts the anagram ahead of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An obliging person is helpful and accommodating, keen to do what is asked.

clue.text: Use this to shift clothes on dollar credit

parts.note: gear is informal for clothes
S stands for the dollar, from the dollar sign
on tick is British slang for on credit

explanation.surface: A tip that one buys outfits on credit using a dollar card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shift clothes' reads as selling clothes, but the definition is changing gear in a car. Buying 'on tick' is British slang for buying on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver moves this lever to change from one gear to another in a car.

clue.text: London dock storing the right gift paper

indicators.note: storing means holding inside, so the dock contains the letter

parts.note: Wapping is a district of East London once famous for its docks
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A London dockside warehouse holds the correct paper for presents.
explanation.walkthrough: WAPPING is an area of East London beside the Thames, historically home to busy docks.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative sheets used to cover a present are known by this name.

clue.text: Beer in tea?

parts.note: being in means being at home
a brew is British slang for a cup of tea

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether there is beer in someone's cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link meaning inside, but it supplies HOME, as in staying in. A 'brew' is British slang for a pot or cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale made by amateurs in their own kitchen is beer brewed domestically.

clue.text: No let-up worrying rich

indicators.note: worrying means troubling or shaking up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Constant anxiety about being wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulent means lavishly wealthy and luxurious.

clue.text: Loving to have trouble on call

parts.note: ado means fuss or trouble
to ring someone is to call them

explanation.surface: Being fond of someone means putting up with nuisance calls.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts ADO above RING.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoring means devoted and full of love.

clue.text: The Spanish act on road repairs in fabulous country

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the
to do is to act or perform

indicators.note: repairs means fixes by reworking, so the letters of road are rearranged

explanation.surface: Spanish workers carry out roadworks in a fairy-tale land.
explanation.definitionFit: This legendary city of gold sought by Spanish explorers is a mythical land of riches, a fabulous country.

clue.text: Tragedies requiring whisky, perhaps a second

parts.note: a dram is a small measure of spirit, especially whisky

explanation.surface: Disasters prompting the need for a quick shot of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tragedies' suggests disasters needing a stiff drink; here it means stage plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragedies are a kind of serious play, so they are examples of stage works of that broader category.

clue.text: Come to a stop and reverse

indicators.note: and reverse tells the solver the letters read the same when turned round

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Instructions to a driver to halt and back up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' looks like a second driving instruction; it says the answer is a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver halting a vehicle draws it to a halt, which is what pulling up means.

clue.text: Sponge and fruit pudding came up with a following

indicators.note: following puts the letter after the reversed pudding
in a down clue came up means the word is read upwards

parts.note: a fool is a dessert of puréed fruit and cream

explanation.surface: A cake and a fruit dessert were served with something to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'came up' means read upwards, and 'a following' tacks on the article last. A fool is a British dessert of fruit folded into cream.
explanation.definitionFit: This dried fibrous gourd is used in the bath for scrubbing, as a sponge is.

clue.text: Vehicles used to pull wagon up hills

indicators.note: up says the word for wagon is turned round and read the other way

parts.note: a cart is a wagon
tors are rocky hills, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Horses or machines are used to haul a cart uphill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns CART into TRAC. A tor is a rocky hilltop, common in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm machines built to haul ploughs and trailers are vehicles designed for pulling.

clue.text: His model is designed to destroy

indicators.note: designed means newly arranged, so the letters are reworked into a new pattern

explanation.surface: An architect's model is built to knock something down.
explanation.definitionFit: To demolish is to pull down or wreck completely, a synonym of destroy.

clue.text: Mysterious articles surrounding Catholic point

indicators.note: surrounding means the articles go round the word for Catholic

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
an is the other form of the indefinite article
RC is short for Roman Catholic
E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Obscure grammar rules about articles near a Catholic topic.
explanation.walkthrough: The two forms of the indefinite article wrap round the Catholic abbreviation, and a compass point ends the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcane means understood by few, so secret or obscure in the same way as mysterious.

clue.text: Pupil dropping out of Boston perhaps is a foreigner

indicators.note: dropping out of says one letter leaves the longer word

parts.note: the Boston Strangler was a notorious killer, one example of a strangler
L stands for learner, a pupil, from the L-plate

explanation.surface: A student quitting a Boston school is someone from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boston perhaps' is a definition by example: the Boston Strangler was a 1960s serial killer. 'Pupil dropping out' suggests a school dropout.
explanation.definitionFit: A stranger is someone unfamiliar, and in older usage a person from another country.
